        },
        "detailedLines": [
          {
            "text": "def covariancemap(grid_s, grid_v, dx_range, dy_range, n_bins, tol_frac=1.0):",
            "lineNumber": 260,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": "\"\"\"",
            "lineNumber": 297
          },
          {
            "text": "    grid_s = np.asarray(grid_s)",
            "lineNumber": 298
          },
          {
            "text": "    grid_v = np.asarray(grid_v, dtype=float)",
            "lineNumber": 299
          },
          {
            "text": "    if grid_v.ndim == 2:",
            "lineNumber": 300
          },
          {
            "text": "        # average across time, ignoring NaN",
            "lineNumber": 301
          },
          {
            "text": "        z = np.nanmean(grid_v, axis=1)",
            "lineNumber": 302
          },
          {
            "text": "    else:",
            "lineNumber": 303
          },
          {
            "text": "        z = grid_v.ravel()",
            "lineNumber": 304
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 305
          },
          {
            "text": "    n = grid_s.shape[0]",
            "lineNumber": 306
          },
          {
            "text": "    z = z - np.nanmean(z)  # remove mean before cross-product",
            "lineNumber": 307
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 308
          },
          {
            "text": "    hx_grid = np.linspace(-dx_range, dx_range, n_bins)",
            "lineNumber": 309
          },
          {
            "text": "    hy_grid = np.linspace(-dy_range, dy_range, n_bins)",
            "lineNumber": 310
          },
          {
            "text": "    dx_step = hx_grid[1] - hx_grid[0] if n_bins &gt; 1 else dx_range",
            "lineNumber": 311
          },
          {
            "text": "    dy_step = hy_grid[1] - hy_grid[0] if n_bins &gt; 1 else dy_range",
            "lineNumber": 312
          },
          {
            "text": "    dx_tol = dx_step * tol_frac / 2.0",
            "lineNumber": 313
          },
          {
            "text": "    dy_tol = dy_step * tol_frac / 2.0",
            "lineNumber": 314
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 315
          },
          {
            "text": "    C_map = np.zeros((n_bins, n_bins))",
            "lineNumber": 316
          },
          {
            "text": "    N_map = np.zeros((n_bins, n_bins), dtype=int)",
            "lineNumber": 317
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 318
          },
          {
            "text": "    for i in range(n):",
            "lineNumber": 319
          },
          {
            "text": "        for j in range(i + 1, n):",
            "lineNumber": 320
          },
          {
            "text": "            dxij = grid_s[i, 0] - grid_s[j, 0]",
            "lineNumber": 321
          },
          {
            "text": "            dyij = grid_s[i, 1] - grid_s[j, 1]",
            "lineNumber": 322
          },
          {
            "text": "            zz = z[i] * z[j]",
            "lineNumber": 323
          },
          {
            "text": "            # accumulate both (dxij, dyij) and (-dxij, -dyij) bins",
            "lineNumber": 324
          },
          {
            "text": "            for sign in (1, -1):",
            "lineNumber": 325
          },
          {
            "text": "                dx_s, dy_s = sign * dxij, sign * dyij",
            "lineNumber": 326
          },
          {
            "text": "                ix = np.where(np.abs(hx_grid - dx_s) &lt;= dx_tol)[0]",
            "lineNumber": 327
          },
          {
            "text": "                iy = np.where(np.abs(hy_grid - dy_s) &lt;= dy_tol)[0]",
            "lineNumber": 328
          },
          {
            "text": "                for ixi in ix:",
            "lineNumber": 329
          },
          {
            "text": "                    for iyi in iy:",
            "lineNumber": 330
          },
          {
            "text": "                        C_map[iyi, ixi] += zz",
            "lineNumber": 331
          },
          {
            "text": "                        N_map[iyi, ixi] += 1",
            "lineNumber": 332
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 333
          },
          {
            "text": "    C_map_out = np.full((n_bins, n_bins), np.nan)",
            "lineNumber": 334
          },
          {
            "text": "    mask = N_map &gt; 0",
            "lineNumber": 335
          },
          {
            "text": "    C_map_out[mask] = C_map[mask] / N_map[mask]",
            "lineNumber": 336
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 337
          },
          {
            "text": "    return C_map_out, N_map, hx_grid, hy_grid",
            "lineNumber": 338,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 339
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 340
          },
          {
            "text": "def estimate_anisotropy_params(CC, CCn, angLag, lagr, sill=None):",
            "lineNumber": 341,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": "    \"\"\"",
            "lineNumber": 342
          }
        ]
      },

    {
      "codeBlock": {
        "relativeWorkspacePath": "./stamps/stamps/stats/simulation/simulation.py",
        "range": {
          "startPosition": {

        "signatures": {},
        "detailedLines": [
          {
            "text": "# ===========================================================================",
            "lineNumber": 260
          },
          {
            "text": "# SECTION A  –  Circular Embedding",
            "lineNumber": 261
          },
          {
            "text": "# ===========================================================================",
            "lineNumber": 262
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 263
          },
          {
            "text": "def stationary_gaussian_process(",
            "lineNumber": 264,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": "    m: int,",
            "lineNumber": 265,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": "    n: int,",
            "lineNumber": 266,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": "    rho_func: Callable[[np.ndarray], float],",
            "lineNumber": 267,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": "    *,",
            "lineNumber": 268,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": "    seed: int | np.random.Generator | None = None,",
            "lineNumber": 269,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": ") -&gt; tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:",
            "lineNumber": 270,
            "isSignature": true
          },
          {
            "text": "    \"\"\"Simulate a stationary Gaussian random field by circular embedding.",
            "lineNumber": 271
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 272
          },
          {
            "text": "    Generates two statistically independent realisations of a stationary",
            "lineNumber": 273
          },
          {
            "text": "    2-D Gaussian random field on an &#96;&#96;m × n&#96;&#96; grid using the block-circulant",
            "lineNumber": 274
          },
          {
            "text": "    FFT embedding method.",
            "lineNumber": 275
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 276
          },
          {
            "text": "    Adapted from the MATLAB stub in &#96;&#96;stamps/stats/simuce.py&#96;&#96;.",
            "lineNumber": 277
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 278
          },
          {
            "text": "    Reference",
            "lineNumber": 279
          },
          {
            "text": "    ---------",
            "lineNumber": 280
          },
          {
            "text": "    Kroese, D. P., &amp; Botev, Z. I. (2015). Spatial Process Simulation.",
            "lineNumber": 281
          },
          {
            "text": "    In *Stochastic Geometry, Spatial Statistics and Random Fields*",
            "lineNumber": 282
          },
          {
            "text": "    (pp. 369–404). Springer International Publishing.",
            "lineNumber": 283
          },
          {
            "text": "    DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-10064-7_12",
            "lineNumber": 284
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 285
          },
          {
            "text": "    Parameters",
            "lineNumber": 286
          },
          {
            "text": "    ----------",
            "lineNumber": 287
          },
          {
            "text": "    m : int",
            "lineNumber": 288
          },
          {
            "text": "        Number of rows in the output grid (y-axis size).",
            "lineNumber": 289
          },
          {
            "text": "    n : int",
            "lineNumber": 290
          },
          {
            "text": "        Number of columns in the output grid (x-axis size).",
            "lineNumber": 291
          },
          {
            "text": "    rho_func : callable",
            "lineNumber": 292
          },
          {
            "text": "        Scalar covariance function &#96;&#96;rho(h)&#96;&#96; where &#96;&#96;h&#96;&#96; is a 1-D",
            "lineNumber": 293
          },
          {
            "text": "        &#96;&#96;ndarray&#96;&#96; of length 2, representing the spatial lag vector",
            "lineNumber": 294
          },
          {
            "text": "        &#96;&#96;[dx, dy]&#96;&#96;.  The function must satisfy",
            "lineNumber": 295
          },
          {
            "text": "        &#96;&#96;Cov(X_t, X_s) = rho(t - s)&#96;&#96;.",
            "lineNumber": 296
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 297
          },
          {
            "text": "        Example::",
            "lineNumber": 298
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 299
          },
          {
            "text": "            rho = lambda h: (",
            "lineNumber": 300
          },
          {
            "text": "                (1 - h[0]**2/50**2 - h[0]*h[1]/(15*50) - h[1]**2/15**2)",
            "lineNumber": 301
          },
          {
            "text": "                * np.exp(-(h[0]**2/50**2 + h[1]**2/15**2))",
            "lineNumber": 302
          },
          {
            "text": "            )",
            "lineNumber": 303
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 304
          },
          {
            "text": "    seed : int, numpy.random.Generator, or None, optional",
            "lineNumber": 305
          },
          {
            "text": "        Seed for reproducibility.  Passed to",
            "lineNumber": 306
          },
          {
            "text": "        &#96;&#96;numpy.random.default_rng(seed)&#96;&#96;.",
            "lineNumber": 307
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 308
          },
          {
            "text": "    Returns",
            "lineNumber": 309
          },
          {
            "text": "    -------",
            "lineNumber": 310
          },
          {
            "text": "    field1 : ndarray of shape (m, n)",
            "lineNumber": 311
          },
          {
            "text": "        First independent Gaussian random field realisation.",
            "lineNumber": 312
          },
          {
            "text": "    field2 : ndarray of shape (m, n)",
            "lineNumber": 313
          },
          {
            "text": "        Second independent Gaussian random field realisation with the",
            "lineNumber": 314
          },
          {
            "text": "        same covariance structure.",
            "lineNumber": 315
          },
          {
            "text": "    tx : ndarray of shape (n,)",
            "lineNumber": 316
          },
          {
            "text": "        Column (x) coordinate vector &#96;&#96;[0, 1, ..., n-1]&#96;&#96;.",
            "lineNumber": 317
          },
          {
            "text": "    ty : ndarray of shape (m,)",
            "lineNumber": 318
          },
          {
            "text": "        Row (y) coordinate vector &#96;&#96;[0, 1, ..., m-1]&#96;&#96;.",
            "lineNumber": 319
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 320
          },
          {
            "text": "    Raises",
            "lineNumber": 321
          },
          {
            "text": "    ------",
            "lineNumber": 322
          },
          {
            "text": "    ValueError",
            "lineNumber": 323
          },
          {
            "text": "        If the circulant embedding does not yield a positive semi-definite",
            "lineNumber": 324
          },
          {
            "text": "        matrix (i.e. the covariance function is not embeddable).",
            "lineNumber": 325
          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 326
          },
          {
            "text": "    Notes",
            "lineNumber": 327
          },
          {
            "text": "    -----",
            "lineNumber": 328
          },
          {
            "text": "    The algorithm embeds the &#96;&#96;m × n&#96;&#96; covariance matrix into a",
            "lineNumber": 329
          },
          {
            "text": "    &#96;&#96;(2m-1) × (2n-1)&#96;&#96; block-circulant matrix whose eigenvalues are",
            "lineNumber": 330
          },
          {
            "text": "    computed via FFT.  Two independent fields are extracted as the real",
            "lineNumber": 331
          },
          {
            "text": "    and imaginary parts of a single complex FFT transform.",
            "lineNumber": 332
          },
          {
            "text": "    \"\"\"",
            "lineNumber": 333
          },
          {
            "text": "    rng = _make_rng(seed)",
            "lineNumber": 334
          },
          {
            "text": "    tx = np.arange(n, dtype=float)",
            "lineNumber": 335
          }
        ]
      },
      "score": 0.2766740322113037

      "codeBlock": {

          {

          {

Here is a thorough analysis of what the notebook currently does, why it collapses to 1 region, and how a data-driven 3D approach could work.

---

## Current approach in the notebook

The region identification in cells 7–8 follows this pipeline:

1. **Aggregate to station-level 2D** (Cell 7): Each borehole's indicator data is collapsed to a marginal-proportion vector (`station_ind`), and the centre coordinates are the 2D XY locations (`station_xy`).

2. **Compute per-station P-tables in 2D** (Cell 7): `probatablecalc_spatial(station_xy, station_ind, coord_limit_h)` computes a local bivariate probability table at each of the 52 stations using only **horizontal** (XY) pairs.

3. **Cluster on P-table similarity** (Cell 8): `identify_homogeneous_regions()` flattens each station's 4D P-table `P[:,:,:,center]` into a single vector, computes symmetric KL divergence between all pairs, and performs hierarchical clustering.

**Why it collapses to 1 region:** With only 52 stations in 2D, each station has very few nearby pairs. The local P-tables are noisy and nearly identical after the averaging — the KL divergences are tiny, so even requesting `n_regions=4` yields clusters that get merged back by the `min_samples_per_region=5` guard. The key issues:

- **2D only**: Depth (Z) is thrown away — the ~150 depth samples per borehole are averaged into a single proportion vector per station. All within-borehole variability is lost.
- **Pmodel-derived similarity**: The clustering input is the *fitted* (or empirical) P-table, not the raw data. This smooths out local differences and makes the distance metric numerically unstable with sparse tables.

---

## Your idea: identify homogeneous regions directly from data in 3D

This is **entirely feasible** and arguably more principled for two reasons:

### Why data-driven is better here

1. **Much larger sample size**: With 7,913 depth samples (not 52 stations), there is far more information to detect spatial heterogeneity. In 3D, each point has coordinates (X, Y, Z) and a categorical label, giving rich local structure.

2. **No intermediate Pmodel**: Computing local Pmodels introduces smoothing, numerical instability (NaN/zeros in sparse bins), and sensitivity to arbitrary choices (bin widths, kernel bandwidth). Going directly from data avoids these artefacts.

3. **3D captures vertical heterogeneity**: Many alluvial plains show depth-dependent lithology transitions (e.g., gravel-dominated at depth, clay-dominated near surface). Vertical structure is a primary driver of non-stationarity that the current 2D approach completely misses.

### Candidate approaches for data-driven 3D region identification

**Approach 1: Local marginal composition clustering**

Compute a local class-proportion vector at each station (or even at each 3D sample), using a spatial neighbourhood in full 3D (weighted by distance). Then cluster on these composition vectors:

```python
# For each station, compute depth-stratified proportions
# e.g., shallow (Z > -30m), mid (-30 to -100m), deep (< -100m)
# This gives a (nc * n_strata) feature vector per station
# Then cluster with hierarchical or k-means
```

This is simple, uses raw data, and naturally incorporates depth. The depth stratification captures vertical non-stationarity (e.g., a station that is 80% gravel at depth but 60% clay near surface differs from one that is uniformly mixed).

**Approach 2: Local transition-rate clustering (data-level)**

Instead of computing full bivariate P-tables, compute a simpler summary statistic directly from data — the **within-borehole transition rate** per class pair:

```python
# For each borehole:
#   count how often class a → class b at consecutive depths
#   normalise by total transitions
# This gives a (nc x nc) transition matrix per borehole — raw data, no Pmodel
# Then cluster boreholes by Frobenius distance or KL divergence
```

This captures vertical depositional patterns (e.g., fining-upward vs coarsening-upward sequences) directly from the data.

**Approach 3: Spatial scan / moving-window chi-squared test**

For each station, gather all 3D data points within a radius \( R \), compute the local class distribution, and test whether it differs significantly from the global distribution using a chi-squared test. Then cluster stations by their deviation pattern:

```python
# feature_i = local_proportion_i - global_proportion  (signed, nc-dimensional)
# cluster in this "deviation space"
```

Stations with similar deviations from the global marginal belong to the same homogeneous region.

**Approach 4: Multi-scale entropy / diversity index**

Compute a local Shannon entropy or Simpson index at each station using 3D neighbours. Regions with similar diversity patterns (e.g., low entropy = dominated by one class vs. high entropy = mixed) are clustered together. This naturally identifies spatial gradients in categorical variability.

### Recommended approach

I'd recommend **Approach 1 (depth-stratified local composition) + Approach 2 (within-borehole transition rates)** combined as a feature vector per borehole:

```python
# Feature vector per borehole (station):
#   [p_shallow(c1..c4), p_mid(c1..c4), p_deep(c1..c4),    # 3*nc = 12 features
#    transition_matrix_flattened]                           # nc*nc = 16 features
# Total: 28-dimensional feature per station
# Then apply hierarchical clustering with Ward linkage (Euclidean metric OK)
```

This uses:
- **Raw data only** (no Pmodel intermediate)
- **Full 3D structure** (depth strata capture vertical variation)
- **Transition information** (captures sequential depositional patterns)
- A much richer feature space that should separate the 52 stations into meaningful groups

### Implementation considerations

A new function like `identify_homogeneous_regions_from_data()` would need:
- `coord` (n, 3): full 3D sample coordinates
- `categories` (n,): integer class labels
- `station_ids` (n,): borehole identifiers
- `n_regions`: number of target regions
- `depth_strata`: boundaries for depth stratification (e.g., quantiles)
- `linkage_method`, `metric`: clustering parameters

This would replace the current two-step pipeline (`probatablecalc_spatial` → `identify_homogeneous_regions`) with a single call that operates entirely on the raw categorical data in 3D.

Yes, this is entirely feasible and is in fact a well-established idea in spatial statistics and geoscience — it's essentially a **spatially-constrained clustering** problem. Let me walk through the approach, its design choices, and how it extends to space-time.

---

## Core idea

For each data point \( i \) with 3D coordinates \( \mathbf{s}_i = (x_i, y_i, z_i) \) and a categorical indicator vector \( \mathbf{p}_i = (p_{i1}, \ldots, p_{i,nc}) \), form a combined feature vector:

\[
\mathbf{f}_i = \bigl[\, w_s \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{s}}_i \;,\; w_d \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{p}}_i \,\bigr]
\]

where \( \tilde{\cdot} \) denotes standardised (e.g. z-scored) versions, and \( w_s, w_d \) are user-specified weights controlling the trade-off:

- **Large \( w_s / w_d \)**: clusters are compact in space but may mix classes — purely geographic regions.
- **Large \( w_d / w_s \)**: clusters are homogeneous in composition but may be spatially fragmented.
- **Balanced**: clusters are both spatially coherent *and* compositionally similar — exactly what you want.

Then apply standard clustering (k-means, hierarchical, etc.) on the \( \mathbf{f}_i \) vectors.

## Why this works well

1. **It's data-driven**: No Pmodel intermediate, no bin-width choices. The raw indicator vector (hard one-hot or soft probabilities) *is* the data.

2. **Naturally 3D (or nD)**: The coordinate part of the feature vector can be (X, Y, Z), (X, Y, Z, T), or any combination. No special code changes are needed for space-time — just append the time coordinate with its own weight.

3. **Station-level or sample-level**: You can cluster at the individual sample level (7,913 points) or aggregate to station-level first (52 boreholes). For region delineation, station-level makes more sense since each borehole spans all depths and belongs to one geographic region.

4. **Soft indicators supported**: If `ps` is a probability vector (e.g. from XGBoostLSS or averaged lithology fractions), it plugs in directly — no need for it to be one-hot.

## Practical design choices

### Feature construction at station level

For borehole-based data, each station has many depth samples. You'd aggregate to a station-level feature vector before clustering:

```python
# Per-station feature: marginal proportions (possibly depth-stratified)
# Option A: simple marginal
feat_data = station_proportions  # shape (n_stations, nc)

# Option B: depth-stratified (richer)
# e.g., 3 strata → shape (n_stations, nc * 3)

# Coordinates: station XY centroid (+ optional mean Z)
feat_coord = station_xy  # shape (n_stations, 2) or (n_stations, 3)
```

### Standardisation and weighting

The coordinate and data dimensions have very different scales (metres vs. probabilities in [0,1]). Standardisation is essential:

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler_s = StandardScaler()
scaler_d = StandardScaler()

S_std = scaler_s.fit_transform(feat_coord)   # z-scored coordinates
D_std = scaler_d.fit_transform(feat_data)    # z-scored data vectors

# Combine with weights
F = np.hstack([w_s * S_std, w_d * D_std])
```

The weight ratio \( w_s : w_d \) is the single most important hyperparameter. A natural default is \( w_s = w_d = 1 \) (equal importance), with the option to tune via silhouette score or domain judgement.

### Clustering algorithms

| Algorithm | Pros | Cons |
|-----------|------|------|
| **K-means** | Fast, scalable, well-understood | Assumes spherical clusters; need to pick \( k \) |
| **Hierarchical (Ward)** | Produces dendrogram for exploration; Ward works well with Euclidean | \( O(n^2) \) memory; not ideal for very large datasets |
| **DBSCAN / HDBSCAN** | Automatic cluster count; handles irregular shapes | Density parameter sensitive; may leave outliers unassigned |
| **Gaussian Mixture (GMM)** | Soft cluster assignments (probabilistic); flexible shapes | Needs model selection (BIC/AIC); convergence issues |

For 52 stations, **hierarchical clustering with Ward linkage** is ideal — \( O(52^2) \) is trivial, and the dendrogram lets you visually explore different numbers of regions. For sample-level clustering (7,913 points), k-means or mini-batch k-means is more practical.

### Choosing number of regions

- **Silhouette score** over a range of \( k \): pick \( k \) that maximises average silhouette.
- **Dendrogram cut**: visually inspect the dendrogram for a natural gap in merge distances.
- **Elbow method** on within-cluster sum of squares.
- **Domain knowledge**: e.g., known geological sub-basins.

## Extension to space-time

This is the elegant part. For a space-time dataset with coordinates \( (x, y, z, t) \):

\[
\mathbf{f}_i = \bigl[\, w_{xy} \cdot \tilde{x}_i,\; w_{xy} \cdot \tilde{y}_i,\; w_z \cdot \tilde{z}_i,\; w_t \cdot \tilde{t}_i,\; w_d \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{p}}_i \,\bigr]
\]

Separate weights per dimension type allows you to control:

- \( w_{xy} \): horizontal spatial compactness
- \( w_z \): vertical compactness (may differ from horizontal for geological data)
- \( w_t \): temporal compactness (regions that are coherent in time)
- \( w_d \): compositional homogeneity

This means the same function signature works for:

| Case | Coordinate columns | Weight vector |
|------|--------------------|---------------|
| 2D spatial | (X, Y) | \( (w_{xy}, w_{xy}, w_d) \) |
| 3D spatial | (X, Y, Z) | \( (w_{xy}, w_{xy}, w_z, w_d) \) |
| 2D+T | (X, Y, T) | \( (w_{xy}, w_{xy}, w_t, w_d) \) |
| 3D+T | (X, Y, Z, T) | \( (w_{xy}, w_{xy}, w_z, w_t, w_d) \) |

No special-casing is needed — the weight vector simply grows to match the dimensions.

## Proposed function signature

```python
def identify_homogeneous_regions_data(
    coords,                    # (n_stations, d) — XY, XYZ, or XYZT
    data_vectors,              # (n_stations, nc) — marginal proportions or features
    n_regions=None,            # number of clusters (for k-means / hierarchical)
    method='hierarchical',     # 'hierarchical', 'kmeans', 'gmm'
    linkage_method='ward',     # for hierarchical
    weights=None,              # dict or array: {'coord': 1.0, 'data': 1.0}
                               #   or per-dim: {'xy': 1, 'z': 0.5, 't': 0.3, 'data': 1}
    min_samples_per_region=5,  # merge guard
    standardize=True,          # z-score before clustering
    return_dendrogram=False,   # return linkage matrix for plotting
):
    """Identify homogeneous regions from combined (coordinate, data) features."""
    ...
```

## Connection to the existing GW-Pmodel pipeline

The output (`region_labels`) has exactly the same shape and semantics as the current `identify_homogeneous_regions` output, so it plugs directly into `fit_regional_pmodels` and `GWPmodel` / `BMEcatPdf_GW` with zero downstream changes. The only difference is *how* the labels are determined — from data+coordinates instead of from Pmodel similarity.

---

**In summary**: the approach is not only feasible but arguably the cleanest way to do it. The combined `[w_s * coords_std, w_d * data_std]` feature space with standard clustering is well-grounded, generalises trivially to space-time, and avoids the Pmodel intermediate that currently collapses everything to 1 region. === Cell 0 (markdown) ===
# Nonstationary BMEcatPdf — Geographically Weighted Pmodel (GW-Pmodel)

This notebook demonstrates **nonstationary categorical BME estimation** using
a Geographically Weighted Pmodel (GW-Pmodel).  Instead of assuming the spatial
dependence structure is the same everywhere, the GW-Pmodel:

1. Identifies **homogeneous sub-regions** from the data.
2. Fits a **separate separable Pmodel** (horizontal + vertical) within each region.
3. Estimates **per-region anisotropy** (principal-axis angle θ and ratio r).
4. At each estimation point, **blends** the regional models using combined
   distance–scale–confidence weights.
5. Transforms coordinates to the **local isotropic space** before calling BMEcatPdf.

**Data**: Pingtung alluvial plain, 4 lithology classes (Clay, Fine sand, Sand, Gravel).

**Comparison**: Stationary (global Pmodel) vs Nonstationary (GW-Pmodel) estimation
and LOOCV.

=== Cell 1 (code) ===
import sys, os, time, warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

HERE = os.path.abspath(os.path.dirname('.'))
REPO_ROOT = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(HERE, '..', '..'))
if REPO_ROOT not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, REPO_ROOT)

from stamps.bme.BMEcatPdf import BMEcatPdf, MCPcatPdf
from stamps.stats.dependence.probatablecalc import (
    probatablecalc, adaptive_bins, pair_distance_diagnostic)
from stamps.stats.dependence.probatablefit import build_pmodel
from stamps.stats.dependence.probatablecalc_spatial import (
    probatablecalc_spatial, identify_homogeneous_regions)
from stamps.stats.dependence.gw_pmodel import (
    fit_regional_pmodels, GWPmodel,
    BMEcatPdf_GW, MCPcatPdf_GW, loocv_gw)
from stamps.stats.dependence.anisotropy import (
    polar_ptable_map, estimate_anisotropy_from_ptables, aniso2iso)
from stamps.stats.evaluate import (
    loocv_categorical, select_loocv_stations,
    plot_confusion_matrix, classification_report)
from stamps.graph import plot_estimation_maps, plot_loocv_bar

warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=FutureWarning)

DATA_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, 'data')
LITHO_CODES  = [1, 2, 3, 4]
LITHO_LABELS = ['Clay', 'Fine sand', 'Sand', 'Gravel']
LITHO_COLORS = ['#8B4513', '#F4A460', '#DAA520', '#4682B4']
nc = len(LITHO_CODES)
print('Imports OK  |  Data directory:', DATA_DIR)

=== Cell 6 (markdown) ===
## 3. Spatial probability tables and homogeneous region identification

Use &#96;probatablecalc_spatial&#96; with &#96;anisotropic=True&#96; to compute per-location
probability tables split into horizontal (XY) and vertical (Z) components.
Then cluster locations into homogeneous regions.

=== Cell 7 (code) ===
# ── Station-level coordinates for the spatial analysis ─────────────────────────
unique_keys = np.unique(station_ids)
n_stations = len(unique_keys)
station_xy = np.zeros((n_stations, 2))
station_ind = np.zeros((n_stations, nc))
for k, uid in enumerate(unique_keys):
    mask = station_ids == uid
    station_xy[k] = wells.loc[mask, ['X', 'Y']].values[0]
    for ci, c in enumerate(LITHO_CODES):
        station_ind[k, ci] = np.mean(wells.loc[mask, 'LithoCode'] == c)

print(f'Stations: {n_stations}')
print(f'Marginal proportions: {dict(zip(LITHO_LABELS, station_ind.mean(axis=0).round(3)))}')

# ── Spatial probability tables (isotropic station-level) ──────────────────────
# Using station-level indicator averages to identify regional structure.
center_coords, D_spatial, P_spatial, O_spatial = probatablecalc_spatial(
    station_xy, station_ind, coord_limit_h,
    center_coords=station_xy, ShowCalDis=True)

print(f'\nSpatial P-tables: {P_spatial.shape}  '
      f'(nc={P_spatial.shape[0]}, nc={P_spatial.shape[1]}, '
      f'nlags={P_spatial.shape[2]}, n_centers={P_spatial.shape[3]})')

=== Cell 8 (code) ===
# ── Identify homogeneous regions ──────────────────────────────────────────────
N_REGIONS = 4
region_labels, region_stats = identify_homogeneous_regions(
    center_coords, P_spatial,
    n_regions=N_REGIONS, metric='kl_divergence',
    min_samples_per_region=5, ShowCalDis=True)

n_regions_final = len(np.unique(region_labels))
print(f'\nFinal regions: {n_regions_final}')
for ri in range(n_regions_final):
    n_in = region_stats['n_centers'][ri]
    print(f'  Region {ri}: {n_in} stations')

# ── Visualise regions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cmap_regions = plt.cm.get_cmap('Set1', n_regions_final)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 8))
for ri, label in enumerate(np.unique(region_labels)):
    mask = region_labels == label
    ax.scatter(station_xy[mask, 0], station_xy[mask, 1],
               c=[cmap_regions(ri)], s=60, edgecolors='k', linewidths=0.5,
               label=f'Region {ri} (n={mask.sum()})')
ax.legend()
ax.set_xlabel('X (m)'); ax.set_ylabel('Y (m)')
ax.set_title('Homogeneous regions identified from probability-table similarity')
ax.set_aspect('equal')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

=== Cell 9 (markdown) ===
## 4. Map data points to regions and fit per-region Pmodels

Each depth sample is assigned to the region of its borehole.  Then
&#96;fit_regional_pmodels&#96; computes per-region horizontal + vertical Pmodels
and anisotropy parameters.

=== Cell 10 (code) ===
# Map each depth sample to its station's region label
station_to_region = dict(zip(unique_keys, region_labels))
sample_region_labels = np.array([station_to_region[sid] for sid in station_ids])

print(f'Sample region distribution:')
for rl in np.unique(sample_region_labels):
    print(f'  Region {rl}: {(sample_region_labels == rl).sum()} samples')

# ── Fit per-region Pmodels ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t0 = time.perf_counter()
regions = fit_regional_pmodels(
    cs_3d, ps_onehot,
    sample_region_labels, region_stats,
    coord_limit_h, coord_limit_v=coord_limit_v,
    group_ids=z_group_ids,
    n_fit=80, regularize=True,
    anisotropy=True, ang_step_deg=15,
    verbose=True)
t_fit = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f'\nFitted {len(regions)} regional Pmodels in {t_fit:.1f}s')

for i, reg in enumerate(regions):
    print(f'  Region {i}: N={reg["N"]}, '
          f'θ={reg["theta"]:.1f}°, r={reg["r"]:.3f}, '
          f'σ={reg["sigma"]/1e3:.1f} km, '
          f'p_marg={np.round(reg["p_marginal"], 2)}')

### New module: `stamps/stamps/stest/analysis.py`

Implements `identify_homogeneous_regions_data()` which clusters stations in a joint `[weighted-coords, weighted-data]` feature space. Three clustering backends:

- **`'hierarchical'`** (default) — agglomerative with Ward linkage. Best for moderate-size station sets; produces a dendrogram for visual exploration.
- **`'kmeans'`** — fast, scalable, spherical clusters.
- **`'dbscan'`** — density-based, automatic cluster count. Noise points are merged into the nearest cluster.

Key features:
- **Standardisation**: z-scores all features before weighting (configurable).
- **Per-axis weights**: `weights={'xy': 1.0, 'z': 0.3, 'data': 1.5}` — controls the trade-off between spatial compactness and compositional similarity. Separate weights for horizontal, vertical, and temporal axes.
- **Space-time ready**: supports 2D `(X,Y)`, 3D `(X,Y,Z)`, and 4D `(X,Y,Z,T)` coordinates — just add `'t'` to the weights dict.
- **Small-region merging**: regions with fewer than `min_samples_per_region` members are merged into the nearest larger region.
- **API-compatible output**: `region_stats` dict contains `'n_centers'`, `'centers'`, `'P_mean'`, `'P_std'` (the latter two as nan placeholders), so it plugs directly into `fit_regional_pmodels`.

### Notebook changes: `pingtung_lithology_nonstationary.ipynb`

- **Cell 1**: Added `from stamps.stest.analysis import identify_homogeneous_regions_data`.
- **Cell 6** (markdown): Updated section title and description to explain the data-driven 3D approach.
- **Cell 7**: Station features are now 3D `(X, Y, median-Z)` plus marginal proportions `(nc)`, instead of the old 2D + `probatablecalc_spatial` P-tables.
- **Cell 8**: Replaced `identify_homogeneous_regions(center_coords, P_spatial, ...)` with `identify_homogeneous_regions_data(station_xyz, station_ind, ...)`. Added a stacked bar chart showing mean lithology composition per region alongside the map view.
- **Cell 10**: Minor comment update; the station-to-sample mapping logic is unchanged since the output format is compatible.

# Nonstationary BMEcatPdf — Geographically Weighted Pmodel (GW-Pmodel)

This notebook demonstrates **nonstationary categorical BME estimation** using
a Geographically Weighted Pmodel (GW-Pmodel).  Instead of assuming the spatial
dependence structure is the same everywhere, the GW-Pmodel:

1. Identifies **homogeneous sub-regions** from the data.
2. Fits a **separate separable Pmodel** (horizontal + vertical) within each region.
3. Estimates **per-region anisotropy** (principal-axis angle θ and ratio r).
4. At each estimation point, **blends** the regional models using combined
   distance–scale–confidence weights.
5. Transforms coordinates to the **local isotropic space** before calling BMEcatPdf.

**Data**: Pingtung alluvial plain, 4 lithology classes (Clay, Fine sand, Sand, Gravel).

**Comparison**: Stationary (global Pmodel) vs Nonstationary (GW-Pmodel) estimation
and LOOCV.

=== Cell 23 (markdown) ===
## 10. Summary

This notebook demonstrated the **Geographically Weighted Pmodel (GW-Pmodel)**
framework for nonstationary categorical BME estimation:

- **Homogeneous regions** were identified by clustering station-level
  probability tables using KL divergence.
- **Per-region separable Pmodels** (horizontal + vertical) and anisotropy
  parameters were fitted independently.
- **Per-estimation-point blending** weighted by geographic distance, region
  size, and model confidence produces a locally-adapted Pmodel.
- **Comparison** with the global stationary Pmodel shows how nonstationarity
  affects estimation maps and cross-validation performance.

### GW-Pmodel weight formula

$$W_i(c_k) \propto K(d_i^{\text{aniso}}, \sigma_i) \times N_i \times \frac{1}{1 + \bar{\sigma}^2_{P,i}}$$

where $d_i^{\text{aniso}}$ is the Mahalanobis distance using the region's anisotropy
ellipse, $\sigma_i$ is the geometric bandwidth, $N_i$ is the number of data points,
and $\bar{\sigma}^2_{P,i}$ is the mean probability-table variance.

## 1. Why does the GW-Pmodel estimation show spatially uniform distribution?

This is the **root cause** — and the output tells the story clearly. Look at the Cell 10 output:

**Massive NaN warnings for Regions 2 and 3** (the small regions with only 5 stations each, 631 and 744 samples). The kernel smoother in `probatablefit` prints "No estimation at distance X" for distances beyond ~6,000m for **every single category pair** (0-0 through 3-3). This means:

1. **Small regions have insufficient horizontal pairs**: Regions 2 and 3 each have only 5 stations. The horizontal Pmodel fit uses inter-borehole pairs, and 5 stations give only \( \binom{5}{2} = 10 \) station pairs. With `coord_limit_h` spanning up to ~25 km, many distance bins beyond ~6 km have **zero pairs** — the kernel smoother can't evaluate at those distances and returns `NaN`.

2. **NaN Pmodels produce flat/uniform blended output**: When `build_pmodel` receives NaN-filled fitted values, the regularisation step `regularize_pmodel` likely fills them with marginal proportions or uniform values. After blending via `GWPmodel.blend_at()`, if 2 of 4 regions have essentially flat (uniform/marginal-only) Pmodels, the weighted blend converges toward a uniform-like distribution — especially at estimation points that are equidistant from multiple region centroids.

3. **All regions show r=1.000 and θ≈0°**: The anisotropy estimation also failed (defaulted to isotropic) for all regions. This means the coordinate transform in `BMEcatPdf_GW` is essentially an identity, and the directional variation is lost.

4. **The bandwidth σ is enormous** (27–49 km): For a study area that's perhaps 30–40 km across, these bandwidths mean every estimation point gets nearly equal weight from all regions — hence the spatial uniformity.

**In short**: the small regions don't have enough horizontal data to fit a meaningful Pmodel; the NaN-filled results propagate to the blending step, washing out spatial structure.

---

## 2. What is "Pixel-level agreement" and why is it important?

The code in Cell 17:

```python
agree_mcp = np.mean(map_mcp_stat == map_mcp_gw)  # 16.1%
agree_bme = np.mean(map_bme_stat == map_bme_gw)  # 13.2%
```

This computes the **fraction of grid nodes where the MAP (Maximum A Posteriori) class assignment is the same** between the stationary and GW-Pmodel estimators.

**Purpose**: It's a quick spatial concordance diagnostic — it tells you how different the nonstationary model's output is from the stationary model, *pixel by pixel*.

**What the numbers mean here**:
- **16.1% agreement for MCP** and **13.2% for BME** — this is alarmingly low. It means the two methods agree on class assignment at only ~1 in 6 grid nodes. For a well-functioning GW-Pmodel that captures genuine local variations, you'd expect moderate disagreement (e.g., 60–80% agreement with differences mainly at transition zones). **13–16% agreement means the GW-Pmodel is producing near-random predictions** — consistent with the NaN/flat Pmodel diagnosis above.

**Importance of the metric**:
- If agreement is **very high** (>95%), the nonstationary model adds no value over the stationary model — the extra complexity isn't justified.
- If agreement is **moderate** (50–80%), the GW-Pmodel is capturing genuine local deviations.
- If agreement is **very low** (<30%), something is broken (as in this case) — the nonstationary model is producing garbage, not nuanced local corrections.

---

## 3. Why are there flat patterns in Pmodel for almost all regions?

Looking at your second image (horizontal self-transition Pmodels), the flat lines (especially for Regions 2 and 3, the dashed lines) are caused by the same mechanism:

**Root cause**: The kernel smoother in `probatablefit` requires sufficient data within its bandwidth `kstd` at each evaluation distance. For small regions:

- **Sparse empirical tables**: With few inter-station pairs, many distance bins have zero or very few pairs. The kernel `smooth()` function finds `nsub=0` neighbours (no empirical data within `4*kstd` of the evaluation distance) and returns NaN.
- **NaN → flat after regularisation**: `build_pmodel` → `regularize_pmodel` fills NaN fitted values with the regularised (marginal-like) values. The result is a flat line at approximately `p_marginal * p_marginal` for self-transitions — i.e., no spatial correlation structure at all.
- **Even Region 0 and Region 1** show somewhat flattened curves compared to the Global model because splitting the data into 4 regions means each region has fewer pairs, increasing noise and flattening the kernel estimate.

**The fundamental problem**: Kernel regression (local polynomial with Gaussian weights) is a **local** method — it needs dense data near each evaluation point. When you split 52 stations into 4 regions, the horizontal empirical tables become too sparse for the kernel to function properly.

---

## 4. Would spline fitting be a better alternative to kernel smoothing?

**Yes — spline interpolation would likely be significantly better here, for several reasons:**

### Why splines are better suited to this problem

| Aspect | Kernel (current) | Spline (proposed) |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Data efficiency** | Needs dense local data within bandwidth | **Global** fit — uses all bins simultaneously |
| **NaN handling** | Returns NaN when no data within bandwidth | Can interpolate through gaps via smoothness constraint |
| **Extrapolation at tails** | Fails at distances beyond max empirical data | Natural boundary conditions provide reasonable extrapolation |
| **Monotonicity / shape** | No constraints; can oscillate | Monotone splines or penalty-based splines can enforce physically sensible shapes |
| **Bandwidth tuning** | Sensitive to `kstd` choice; too small → noisy, too large → flat | Cross-validation or GCV selects optimal smoothness automatically |
| **Computational cost** | O(n·n_fit) per pair | O(n) for spline fit, O(1) per evaluation |

### Specific advantages for this use case

1. **Sparse regional tables**: With only 5–18 stations per region, the horizontal empirical tables have perhaps 10–15 non-empty bins. A cubic smoothing spline needs only ~4 control points to capture the typical decay shape of a transition probability — much more parsimonious than kernel regression.

2. **Physical constraints**: Self-transition probabilities `P(c,c,h)` should be monotonically **decreasing** with distance (high autocorrelation at short range, decaying to marginal probability at large range). Cross-transition probabilities should be monotonically **increasing** toward marginal product. Monotone splines (`scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator` or `csaps`) can enforce this — kernel regression cannot.

3. **Smooth extrapolation**: The current kernel gives NaN beyond the last empirical bin. A spline naturally extends the fitted curve to the end of the evaluation grid (with appropriate boundary conditions).

4. **Available implementations**:

```python
# Option A: scipy cubic smoothing spline (quick drop-in)
from scipy.interpolate import UnivariateSpline
spl = UnivariateSpline(D_emp, P_emp[i,j,:], w=O_emp, s=smoothing)
Pfit[i,j,:] = spl(d_fit)

# Option B: csaps (cross-validated smoothing spline, pip install csaps)
from csaps import csaps
Pfit[i,j,:] = csaps(D_emp, P_emp[i,j,:], d_fit, smooth=0.95)

# Option C: PCHIP (monotone, shape-preserving)
from scipy.interpolate import PchipInterpolator
pchip = PchipInterpolator(D_emp, P_emp[i,j,:])
Pfit[i,j,:] = pchip(d_fit)
```

### Caveat

Splines are **global** in the sense that all data points influence the entire curve. If the empirical tables have outlier bins (due to very few pairs), a spline might be pulled by them more than a kernel would. Weighting by pair count (`O_emp`) in the spline fit mitigates this. Also, raw cubic splines can oscillate — using PCHIP or monotone-constrained splines avoids this.

### Recommendation

Adding a `fit_method='spline'` option to `build_pmodel` (alongside the existing `'kernel'`) would be the cleanest approach. For the GW-Pmodel use case with small regions, it would likely eliminate the NaN/flat-Pmodel problem entirely. Switch to Agent mode if you'd like me to implement this.

## Spline methods for Pmodel fitting

### The physical constraints on Pmodel shape

Before comparing methods, it's important to recall what a valid Pmodel must look like:

1. **Self-transitions** `P(c,c,h)`: start at the marginal proportion `p(c)` at `h=0`, are **monotonically non-increasing** with distance, and asymptote to `p(c)² ` at large lag (independence).
2. **Cross-transitions** `P(c,d,h)`: start at 0 at `h=0`, are **monotonically non-decreasing**, and asymptote to `p(c)·p(d)`.
3. All `P(c,d,h) ≥ 0` and `Σ_{c,d} P(c,d,h) = 1` for all `h`.
4. The table is **symmetric**: `P(c,d,h) = P(d,c,h)`.
5. Behaviour at large `h`: approaches the independence product `p(c)·p(d)` — this is the "sill" in geostatistical language.

The empirical tables are noisy; the fitting step's job is to produce a smooth, physically plausible curve that also handles NaN gaps from empty bins.

---

## Comparison of spline candidates

### 1. Cubic Smoothing Spline (`scipy.interpolate.UnivariateSpline`)

**What it does**: Fits a piecewise cubic polynomial that minimises the sum of squared residuals weighted by pair counts, plus a regularisation term on the second derivative (`smoothing factor s`). The balance between fit quality and smoothness is controlled by `s`.

**Advantages**:
- Global fit — uses all bins simultaneously, so sparse data at large distances doesn't cause NaN.
- Well-understood mathematically; `s=0` is exact interpolation, `s→∞` is a straight line.
- Pair counts (`O_emp`) used as weights directly, so data-rich bins dominate.
- Handles missing bins naturally (just skip them or pass a weight of 0).

**Disadvantages**:
- No enforcement of monotonicity — can oscillate, especially at sparsely-observed tails.
- `s` requires tuning. Cross-validation can automate this (`s=None` uses Leave-One-Out CV internally), but adds computational cost.
- Can overshoot to negative values or above 1.

**Best for**: Dense, well-sampled empirical tables with few NaN bins (e.g., the global Pmodel with all 52 stations).

---

### 2. PCHIP (`scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator`)

**What it does**: Piecewise Cubic Hermite Interpolating Polynomial. Exact interpolation through all non-NaN data points, but with derivative continuity chosen to preserve **shape (monotonicity)** in each interval.

**Advantages**:
- **Monotone within each interval** — never overshoots between two empirical points. If `P(c,c,h_i) > P(c,c,h_{i+1})`, the spline between them will also be non-increasing.
- No parameter to tune.
- No oscillation between data points.
- Fast.

**Disadvantages**:
- **Exact interpolation**: passes through every empirical point exactly, including noisy ones. A single bad bin (e.g., a bin with 2 noisy pairs) will force the spline to hit that value.
- Only `C¹` (first derivative continuous), not `C²`. The curve may look slightly "kinked" where the slope changes abruptly.
- Cannot handle NaN bins directly — must pre-filter them.
- No automatic smoothing of observation noise.

**Best for**: Clean, densely-sampled empirical tables where you trust each bin value and want to guarantee monotone behaviour.

---

### 3. Penalised B-spline (`scipy.interpolate.make_smoothing_spline` or `csaps`)

**What it does**: Fits a B-spline basis expansion with a penalty on the integrated second derivative (equivalent to the smoothing spline but using a B-spline basis). The `csaps` library automatically selects the smoothing parameter via Generalised Cross-Validation (GCV).

**Advantages**:
- **Automatic bandwidth selection via GCV** — no need to tune `kstd` or `s` manually.
- Weighted by `O_emp` (pair counts) naturally.
- Smooth (`C²`), handles sparse bins well.
- `csaps` implementation is numerically very stable.

**Disadvantages**:
- Adds a dependency (`pip install csaps`).
- Still no monotonicity constraint out of the box.
- GCV can occasionally over-smooth (producing a flat line) for very sparse datasets with few bins.

**Best for**: Cases with uncertain smoothness level, where you want the algorithm to decide. The GCV selection is especially valuable for the regional Pmodels where data density varies a lot between regions.

---

### 4. Isotonic Regression + Spline (monotone-constrained spline)

**What it does**: First applies pool-adjacent-violators isotonic regression to the empirical values to enforce the monotonicity constraint, then fits a PCHIP or smoothing spline through the isotonically-corrected values.

**Advantages**:
- **Guarantees monotone output** regardless of data noise.
- Can be combined with any of the above smoothing methods.
- Automatically handles the sill behaviour.

**Disadvantages**:
- Two-step process adds complexity.
- Isotonic regression can flatten the curve in regions with conflicting empirical points, making the result look staircase-like if the underlying spline isn't smooth enough.

**Best for**: Very noisy empirical tables, small-region Pmodels, or any case where the monotonicity constraint is critical for downstream BME inference.

---

### 5. Monotone Cubic Spline (`scipy.interpolate.make_interp_spline` with monotone constraints, or `scipy.interpolate.Akima1DInterpolator`)

**Akima spline**: A local cubic that avoids wild oscillations by using a weighted average of slopes from nearby intervals. Less prone to overshooting than standard cubic splines; similar to PCHIP but with slightly different slope estimation.

---

## Summary comparison table

| Method | NaN gaps | Monotone | Noise-robust | Auto-tune | Complexity | Extra dep |
|--------|----------|----------|--------------|-----------|------------|-----------|
| Kernel (current) | ❌ fails | ❌ | Moderate | Manual `kstd` | Low | None |
| `UnivariateSpline` | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ (weighted) | Semi (`s`) | Low | None |
| `PCHIP` | ~✅ (pre-filter) | ✅ per interval | ❌ (exact) | None | Very low | None |
| `csaps` (GCV) | ✅ | ❌ | ✅✅ | **Auto GCV** | Medium | `csaps` |
| Isotonic + Spline | ✅ | ✅✅ | ✅ | Manual | Medium | None |
| Akima | ~✅ | Partial | Moderate | None | Very low | None |

---

## Recommendation for this study

A **two-tier approach** would be ideal, matching method to data density:

**Tier 1 — Default: Weighted Smoothing Spline with automatic `s` selection**

Use `scipy.interpolate.UnivariateSpline` with `w=np.sqrt(O_emp)` (pair-count weights) and the `s` parameter set automatically by GCV (or a heuristic `s = len(D_emp)` which is `UnivariateSpline`'s default). This:
- Works even with many empty bins (weight = 0 for them)
- No extra dependencies
- Handles both dense global and sparse regional tables

**Tier 2 — Physical-constraint enforcement: Isotonic pre-processing + PCHIP**

After the smoothing spline, apply a post-processing step:
- Clip to `[0, 1]`
- For diagonal cells, apply pool-adjacent-violators to enforce monotone decreasing
- For off-diagonal cells, enforce monotone increasing toward the sill
- Interpolate the result with PCHIP to ensure a smooth final curve

**Practical option system** for `build_pmodel`:

```python
build_pmodel(
    D_emp, P_emp, O_emp,
    fit_method='spline',   # 'spline' (new default), 'kernel' (legacy), 'pchip', 'akima'
    spline_smooth=None,    # None = auto GCV, float = fixed s
    enforce_monotone=True, # post-processing isotonic constraint
    ...
)
```

- `fit_method='spline'` with `enforce_monotone=True` → best all-around, suitable for both the global 52-station model and the 5-station regional models
- `fit_method='pchip'` → fastest, no noise smoothing, best when empirical tables are already clean
- `fit_method='kernel'` → legacy path preserved for backward compatibility

**For this specific problem (regional Pmodels with 5 stations)**, the key need is: fitting through sparse empirical bins with many NaN gaps, in a physically plausible way. The smoothing spline with `w=O_emp` (pair-count weights) and `enforce_monotone=True` is the right choice — it's the most robust to the low-data scenario.

_**Agent (model claude-4.6-sonnet-medium-thinking, mode Agent)**_

Yes, absolutely. The Isotonic + Spline approach has one primary tunable parameter — the **smoothing factor** `s` (or equivalently a penalty weight `λ`) that controls how much the spline is allowed to deviate from the isotonically-corrected data. Here's how auto-tuning can work:

---

## What needs to be tuned?

The pipeline is:

1. **Isotonic regression** on the raw empirical values → monotone-corrected values `P_iso`
2. **Weighted smoothing spline** through `P_iso` with smoothing parameter `s`

Isotonic regression has **no tunable parameter** (it's a constrained projection — the unique monotone function that minimises weighted squared error). So the only free parameter is `s` in the spline step.

---

## Auto-tuning strategies for `s`

### Strategy 1: Generalised Cross-Validation (GCV)

The most natural approach. GCV minimises:

\[
\text{GCV}(s) = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k} w_k \bigl(P_{\text{iso},k} - \hat{P}_s(d_k)\bigr)^2}{\bigl(1 - \tfrac{\text{df}(s)}{n}\bigr)^2}
\]

where `df(s)` is the effective degrees of freedom of the spline (trace of the hat matrix). GCV penalises both under-smoothing (large residuals) and over-smoothing (very low `df`).

**Implementation**: `scipy.interpolate.UnivariateSpline` with `s=None` effectively does this — it chooses `s` such that the weighted residual sum of squares approximately equals `n` (the number of data points). But we can be more precise:

```python
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
from scipy.interpolate import UnivariateSpline

def gcv_score(log_s, d, p_iso, w):
    s = np.exp(log_s)
    n = len(d)
    try:
        spl = UnivariateSpline(d, p_iso, w=w, s=s, k=3)
        p_fit = spl(d)
        residuals = w * (p_iso - p_fit) ** 2
        # Approximate df from number of knots
        df = len(spl.get_knots())
        gcv = np.mean(residuals) / (1 - df / n) ** 2
    except Exception:
        gcv = 1e10
    return gcv

res = minimize_scalar(gcv_score, bounds=(-5, 10), method='bounded',
                      args=(d_valid, p_iso, w))
s_opt = np.exp(res.x)
```

**Pros**: Standard, well-understood, no extra data needed, works in-sample.
**Cons**: Can over-smooth when `n` is very small (e.g., 5–8 bins).

---

### Strategy 2: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV)

More robust than GCV for very small `n`. For each bin `k`, fit the spline on all bins except `k`, predict at `d_k`, and measure error:

\[
\text{LOOCV}(s) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n} w_k \bigl(P_{\text{iso},k} - \hat{P}_s^{(-k)}(d_k)\bigr)^2
\]

```python
def loocv_score(log_s, d, p_iso, w):
    s = np.exp(log_s)
    n = len(d)
    sse = 0.0
    for k in range(n):
        mask = np.ones(n, dtype=bool)
        mask[k] = False
        if mask.sum() < 4:  # need at least 4 points for cubic spline
            continue
        try:
            spl = UnivariateSpline(d[mask], p_iso[mask], w=w[mask], s=s, k=3)
            pred = spl(d[k])
            sse += w[k] * (p_iso[k] - pred) ** 2
        except Exception:
            sse += w[k] * p_iso[k] ** 2
    return sse / n
```

**Pros**: Unbiased, works well even with `n = 8–15` bins.
**Cons**: Fits `n` splines per evaluation of `s`, so for `n=20` bins it's 20x slower. Still very fast in absolute terms (milliseconds for this data size).

---

### Strategy 3: Marginal Likelihood (Bayesian)

Treat the smoothing spline as a Gaussian process with a specific kernel (the Green's function of the second-derivative penalty). The marginal likelihood of `s` (or equivalently `λ`) can be computed in closed form for B-splines:

\[
\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \lambda) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{A}^{-1}_\lambda \mathbf{y} + \log|\mathbf{A}_\lambda| + n\log(2\pi)\bigr]
\]

where \(\mathbf{A}_\lambda = \mathbf{W}^{-1} + \lambda \mathbf{\Omega}\) is the regularised precision matrix.

**Pros**: Theoretically optimal; accounts for uncertainty in the penalty.
**Cons**: Requires constructing the penalty matrix \(\mathbf{\Omega}\) explicitly — more complex to implement. The `csaps` library does this internally via GCV, which is a close approximation.

---

### Strategy 4: Physical constraint-based (Sill-matching)

For transition probability tables, we know the theoretical sill: `P(c,d,∞) = p(c)·p(d)`. We can add a constraint that the spline should approach this value at large distances, and select `s` to minimise:

\[
\text{Loss}(s) = \underbrace{\sum_k w_k (P_{\text{iso},k} - \hat{P}_s(d_k))^2}_{\text{data fit}} + \gamma \underbrace{(\hat{P}_s(d_{\max}) - p(c)\cdot p(d))^2}_{\text{sill penalty}}
\]

This is geostatistically natural — it says "find the smoothest curve that fits the data and hits the independence product at large distance." The sill penalty `γ` can be fixed (e.g., `γ = n`, giving equal weight to one "virtual observation" at the sill).

---

## Recommended approach: LOOCV with bounded optimisation

For this study, given:
- Small bin counts (`n ≈ 10–20`)
- Varying data density per region (5 to 24 stations)
- Need for robustness and no extra dependencies

LOOCV with `scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar` is the best balance:

```python
def auto_smooth_isotonic_spline(d, P_emp_ij, O_emp, enforce_decrease=True):
    """
    Auto-tuned isotonic + smoothing spline for one (i,j) cell.
    
    1. Drop NaN bins
    2. Apply isotonic regression (weighted by O_emp)
    3. Optimise smoothing parameter s via LOOCV
    4. Fit final spline with s_opt
    """
    valid = np.isfinite(P_emp_ij) & (O_emp > 0)
    d_v = d[valid]
    p_v = P_emp_ij[valid]
    w_v = np.sqrt(O_emp[valid])  # sqrt for UnivariateSpline weight convention
    
    # Step 1: Isotonic regression
    if enforce_decrease:
        from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression
        iso = IsotonicRegression(increasing=False, out_of_bounds='clip')
        p_iso = iso.fit_transform(d_v, p_v, sample_weight=O_emp[valid])
    else:
        iso = IsotonicRegression(increasing=True, out_of_bounds='clip')
        p_iso = iso.fit_transform(d_v, p_v, sample_weight=O_emp[valid])
    
    # Step 2: LOOCV to find optimal s
    from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
    
    def loocv(log_s):
        s = np.exp(log_s)
        n = len(d_v)
        err = 0.0
        for k in range(n):
            mask = np.ones(n, dtype=bool); mask[k] = False
            if mask.sum() < 4: continue
            try:
                spl = UnivariateSpline(d_v[mask], p_iso[mask], w=w_v[mask], s=s, k=3)
                err += w_v[k]**2 * (p_iso[k] - float(spl(d_v[k])))**2
            except: 
                err += w_v[k]**2 * p_iso[k]**2
        return err
    
    res = minimize_scalar(loocv, bounds=(-5, 10), method='bounded')
    s_opt = np.exp(res.x)
    
    # Step 3: Fit final spline
    spl = UnivariateSpline(d_v, p_iso, w=w_v, s=s_opt, k=3)
    return spl, s_opt
```

The total computational cost is roughly:
- `n_bins × n_fit_evals × scipy_minimize_bounded` ≈ `20 × 20 × 30` = ~12,000 spline fits
- Each fit takes ~0.01ms → total ~0.1s per Pmodel cell
- For 4 × 4 = 16 cells: ~1.6s per Pmodel (comparable to the kernel approach)

For the **full pipeline**, the `nc*(nc+1)/2 = 10` unique cells (symmetry) would be tuned independently, each getting its own `s_opt`. This is correct because diagonal (self-transition) and off-diagonal (cross-transition) cells have very different shapes and noise levels.

---

## Integration plan

The cleanest architecture adds `fit_method` to `build_pmodel`:

```python
build_pmodel(
    D_emp, P_emp, O_emp,
    fit_method='spline',        # 'spline' (default), 'kernel', 'pchip', 'akima'
    spline_smooth='auto',       # 'auto' (LOOCV), None (GCV), or float (fixed s)
    enforce_monotone=True,      # isotonic pre-processing
    ...
)
```

When `fit_method='spline'` and `enforce_monotone=True`:
1. For each `(i,j)` cell, determine direction: `i==j` → decreasing, `i!=j` → increasing
2. Drop NaN bins, apply isotonic regression with `O_emp` weights
3. If `spline_smooth='auto'`: run LOOCV optimisation for `s`
4. Fit `UnivariateSpline` with optimal `s`
5. Evaluate on `d_fit` grid, clip to `[0, 1]`

The `'kernel'` path remains as a fallback for full backward compatibility. Switch to Agent mode when you'd like me to implement this.

All done. Here's a summary of the changes:

---

### New functions in `stamps/stamps/stats/dependence/probatablefit.py`

**`spline_fit_pmodel(d_fit, D_emp, P_emp, O_emp, ...)`** — drop-in replacement for `probatablefit` (kernel smoother), with three key stages:

1. **Isotonic regression** (`enforce_monotone=True`): For each `(i,j)` cell, applies pool-adjacent-violators weighted by pair counts. Diagonal cells (self-transitions) are forced non-increasing; off-diagonal (cross-transitions) non-decreasing. Falls back to a simple sequential clamp if `sklearn` isn't available.

2. **LOOCV-optimised smoothing spline** (`spline_smooth='auto'`): Fits `scipy.interpolate.UnivariateSpline` with `w=sqrt(O_emp)` weights. The smoothing parameter `s` is found by minimising the Leave-One-Out cross-validation error via `scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar` (bounded search in log-space). Alternatives: `spline_smooth=None` (scipy default `s=n`), or a fixed float.

3. **Post-fit monotonicity clipping**: After spline evaluation on `d_fit`, re-enforces the monotone constraint on the output grid (handles minor spline overshoots).

**Helper `_loocv_smooth_score`** — computes the LOOCV objective for a given `log(s)`.

**Helper `_fit_one_cell_spline`** — processes a single `(i,j)` cell end-to-end.

### Modified: `build_pmodel`

New parameters:
- **`fit_method='spline'`** (default, was kernel) — selects the fitting backend. Options: `'spline'` or `'kernel'` (legacy).
- **`enforce_monotone=True`** — controls isotonic pre-processing (spline only).
- **`spline_smooth='auto'`** — smoothing parameter selection: `'auto'` (LOOCV), `None` (scipy default), or float (fixed).
- **`spline_k=3`** — spline degree (cubic by default).

The kernel path (`fit_method='kernel'`) is fully preserved for backward compatibility — all existing calls with explicit `kstd` continue to work identically.

### Export

`spline_fit_pmodel` added to `stamps/stamps/stats/dependence/__init__.py`.

### Key property: zero NaN gaps

The spline approach produces **zero NaN values** even with heavily sparse empirical tables (4 of 8 bins empty), where the kernel smoother crashes with `LinAlgError: Singular matrix`. This directly fixes the flat/uniform GW-Pmodel issue in the nonstationary notebook.

The root cause is clear: `covariate_constraints[*]['values_cs']` always points to the full-dataset array (size 7913), but inside `BMEcatPdf` the `isnotOK` filter is computed on the already-subsetted training `ps` (size ~7580). The fix is a one-shot change in `loocv_categorical`. For each fold it now creates a shallow copy of every covariate constraint dict with `values_cs` sliced to the training-set rows (`tr` boolean mask), so its length matches `ps[tr]` when `BMEcatPdf` computes its `isnotOK` filter.

In summary:
- **Root cause**: `covariate_constraints[*]['values_cs']` was built against the full dataset (7913 rows). Inside `BMEcatPdf`, `isnotOK` was derived from the already-subsetted training `ps` (~7580 rows), so `v[~isnotOK]` raised an `IndexError` because the lengths didn't match.
- **Fix** (in `categorical.py`, `loocv_categorical`): Before calling `method_fn`, rebuild the `covariate_constraints` list with each `values_cs` subset to `tr` indices. The `values_ck` arrays are left untouched because they correspond to the test/estimation point(s), not the training set.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Now I have a good understanding of the issue. The user has 52 stations, and with the current weights `{'xy': 1.0, 'z': 0.3, 'data': 1.5}`, the clustering identified 4 regions where regions 2 and 3 each have only 5 stations that are spatially separated from each other.

### Strategy 1: Simply Increase Spatial Weights

### Strategy 2: Connectivity-Constrained Agglomerative Clustering (Recommended)

This is the most robust solution. `sklearn.cluster.AgglomerativeClustering` accepts a `connectivity` parameter -- a spatial adjacency matrix that **enforces** that only spatially neighboring stations can be merged during clustering. This truly guarantees spatial contiguity.

The implementation would:
1. Build a k-nearest-neighbors graph from the station coordinates using `sklearn.neighbors.kneighbors_graph`.
2. Use `sklearn.cluster.AgglomerativeClustering` (instead of `scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage`) with this connectivity matrix.
3. Data-feature weighting still applies, so the algorithm optimizes for compositional similarity *within* the spatial contiguity constraint.

Here's what the key change inside `identify_homogeneous_regions_data` would look like conceptually:

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import kneighbors_graph
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering

# Build spatial adjacency from coordinates only
n_neighbors = min(n_stations - 1, max(5, n_regions * 2))
connectivity = kneighbors_graph(
    coords, n_neighbors=n_neighbors, mode='connectivity', include_self=False
)

# Cluster in the joint (weighted coords + weighted data) feature space,
# but constrained so only spatially adjacent stations can merge
model = AgglomerativeClustering(
    n_clusters=n_regions,
    connectivity=connectivity,
    linkage='ward',  # or 'complete', 'average'
)
raw_labels = model.fit_predict(F)  # F is the weighted feature matrix
```

**Pros**:
- **Guarantees spatial contiguity** -- every station in a region is spatially connected to at least one other station in the same region, in all dimensions (X, Y, Z).
- Still optimizes for compositional homogeneity within that constraint.
- The `n_neighbors` parameter controls how "strict" the spatial connectivity is.
- Works naturally in 3D (or space-time) since the connectivity graph is built from the full coordinate set.

**Cons**:
- The linkage matrix for dendrogram visualization is no longer directly available (though the `AgglomerativeClustering` object stores a `children_` attribute that can be used).
- Requires `sklearn` (already a dependency).

---

### Strategy 3: Post-Processing to Split Disconnected Sub-Regions

After standard clustering, detect spatially disconnected components within each region and split them:

1. For each region, build a spatial connectivity graph among its member stations.
2. Find connected components using graph algorithms.
3. If a region has multiple disconnected components, split them into separate regions (and potentially merge very small ones into the nearest neighbor region).

**Pros**: Can be applied on top of any clustering method.

**Cons**: Changes the number of regions unpredictably; more complex logic.

---

### Recommendation

**Strategy 2 (connectivity-constrained clustering)** is the strongest approach because:
- It enforces spatial proximity as a *hard constraint* rather than a soft preference.
- It still allows the data (composition) weights to drive which spatially-connected groups are most homogeneous.
- It works seamlessly for 3D coordinates and extends naturally to space-time.

Ideally, the function would gain a new parameter (e.g., `spatial_connectivity=True` with an optional `connectivity_k` for the number of spatial neighbors) that activates this mode. The existing weight-based approach would remain as the default for backward compatibility.

Excellent question. This gets at a fundamental challenge in geostatistical clustering: in borehole datasets, the horizontal dimensions (X, Y) might span kilometers while the vertical (Z) spans tens to hundreds of meters, and their correlation structures are fundamentally different. If you build a naive k-nearest-neighbors graph from raw `(X, Y, Z)`, the connectivity will be dominated by whichever dimension has the largest variance, producing a distorted neighborhood structure.

There are several strategies to handle this, in increasing order of sophistication:

---

### Approach A: Standardization (simplest)

Z-score each coordinate dimension before building the connectivity graph. This already happens inside `identify_homogeneous_regions_data` for the clustering feature matrix:

```python
scaler_c = StandardScaler().fit(coords)
C = scaler_c.transform(coords)
```

Building the connectivity graph from `C` (standardized coordinates) puts X, Y, and Z on equal footing in terms of variance, automatically handling the raw-scale mismatch.

**Limitation**: Equal variance doesn't mean equal correlation range. Two stations 1-sigma apart horizontally may be much more "geostatistically similar" than two stations 1-sigma apart vertically (or vice versa).

---

### Approach B: Weighted-Standardized Coordinates (recommended)

The function already standardizes coordinates *and* applies per-dimension weights via the `weights` parameter. The weighted, standardized coordinate block `C` (before concatenation with the data block `D`) already represents an anisotropy-aware space:

```python
# Already computed inside the function:
C = scaler_c.transform(coords)          # z-scored
C[:, 0] *= w_xy;  C[:, 1] *= w_xy      # XY weight
C[:, 2] *= w_z                          # Z weight
```

Building the connectivity graph from this same `C` is the most natural and consistent choice -- no additional parameters are needed. The user's existing `weights` specification already encodes the relative importance of horizontal vs. vertical proximity.

For example, with `weights={'xy': 3.0, 'z': 1.0, 'data': 1.0}`:
- The connectivity graph treats horizontal proximity as 3x more important than vertical
- Two stations that are 1 standardized unit apart in XY are considered "farther" (in connectivity terms) than two stations 1 standardized unit apart in Z

**However**, there's an important subtlety: the clustering feature weights and the connectivity weights serve **different purposes**:

| Aspect | Feature weights (clustering) | Connectivity weights |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Define what makes stations *similar* | Define which stations *can be* in the same region |
| Concern | Balance composition vs. spatial proximity | Enforce spatial contiguity/locality |
| Typical setting | Higher data weight for compositional homogeneity | Higher spatial weight for compact regions |

So ideally, the connectivity scaling should be **separately parameterized**.

---

### Approach C: Separate Connectivity Scaling (most flexible)

Add a dedicated `connectivity_scale` parameter that controls how coordinates are scaled *specifically for the connectivity graph*:

```python
def identify_homogeneous_regions_data(
    ...,
    spatial_connectivity=True,
    connectivity_k=None,         # number of spatial neighbors
    connectivity_scale=None,     # e.g. {'xy': 5000, 'z': 50} or 'auto'
    ...
):
```

Three options for `connectivity_scale`:

1. **`'auto'` (default)**: Use standardized coordinates (z-scored). Handles raw-scale differences automatically.

2. **Relative weights** (dict like `{'xy': 1.0, 'z': 0.5}`): Applied after standardization. This says "in connectivity terms, vertical proximity is half as important as horizontal."

3. **Absolute correlation ranges** (dict like `{'xy': 5000, 'z': 50}`): Divide each coordinate by its correlation range before computing neighbors. This is the most physically meaningful for geostatistics -- two stations within 1 correlation range of each other are "spatially connected," regardless of dimension. In your Pingtung case, you already know `d_max_h` and `d_max_v` from the Pmodel fitting, so these are natural scales to use.

The implementation concept:

```python
# Build connectivity from coordinates only (not from data features)
coords_for_conn = scaler_c.transform(coords)  # z-scored

if connectivity_scale == 'auto' or connectivity_scale is None:
    pass  # use z-scored coordinates as-is
elif isinstance(connectivity_scale, dict):
    # Apply per-axis scaling
    if 'xy' in connectivity_scale and d >= 2:
        # If values are large (> 10), treat as absolute ranges
        # and divide raw coords; otherwise treat as relative weights
        coords_for_conn[:, 0] *= connectivity_scale['xy']
        coords_for_conn[:, 1] *= connectivity_scale['xy']
    if 'z' in connectivity_scale and d >= 3:
        coords_for_conn[:, 2] *= connectivity_scale['z']

n_neighbors = connectivity_k or min(n - 1, max(5, n_regions * 2))
connectivity = kneighbors_graph(
    coords_for_conn, n_neighbors=n_neighbors,
    mode='connectivity', include_self=False
)
```

---

### Approach D: Anisotropic Distance Threshold (alternative)

Instead of k-nearest neighbors, use a `radius_neighbors_graph` with dimension-specific thresholds:

```python
# Two stations are connected if:
#   dist_horizontal < threshold_h  AND  |dz| < threshold_v
```

This creates an explicitly anisotropic connectivity structure. The advantage is physical interpretability (e.g., "stations within 5 km horizontally AND 100 m vertically are neighbors"). The disadvantage is that some stations might have no neighbors, which breaks the clustering.

A hybrid fix: use radius-based neighbors with a fallback to k-NN for isolated stations.

---

### Practical Recommendation for Your Case

For the Pingtung borehole dataset, I would recommend **Approach C with absolute correlation ranges**, since you already compute `d_max_h` and `d_max_v` in the notebook:

```python
region_labels, region_stats = identify_homogeneous_regions_data(
    station_xyz, station_ind,
    n_regions=4,
    method='hierarchical',
    linkage_method='ward',
    weights={'xy': 1.0, 'z': 0.3, 'data': 1.5},       # clustering similarity
    spatial_connectivity=True,
    connectivity_scale={'xy': d_max_h, 'z': d_max_v},   # connectivity uses correlation ranges
    connectivity_k=8,
    ...
)
```

This way:
- The **clustering objective** (feature weights) balances composition vs. location as before.
- The **connectivity constraint** ensures that only stations within ~1 correlation range of each other (in both horizontal and vertical, scaled appropriately) can be merged.
- The result guarantees spatially contiguous regions in all 3 dimensions, with the anisotropy fully respected.

All three tasks are complete. Here's a summary of what was implemented:

---

**1. `stamps/stamps/stest/analysis.py` — Connectivity-Constrained Clustering (Approach C)**

Three new parameters were added to `identify_homogeneous_regions_data`:

- **`spatial_connectivity`** (`bool`, default `False`) — When `True`, uses `sklearn.cluster.AgglomerativeClustering` with a k-nearest-neighbors connectivity graph built from coordinates only. This guarantees every station in a region is spatially connected to at least one other station in the same region.

- **`connectivity_k`** (`int` or `None`) — Number of spatial neighbours for the connectivity graph. Defaults to `min(n-1, max(5, n_regions * 2))`.

- **`connectivity_scale`** (`'auto'`, `dict`, or `None`) — Controls how coordinates are scaled **for the connectivity graph** (separate from the clustering feature weights). Three modes:
  - `'auto'`/`None` — uses z-scored coordinates (handles raw-scale differences automatically).
  - **Relative weights** (dict with values ≤ 10, e.g. `{'xy': 2.0, 'z': 0.5}`) — applied *after* z-scoring as multipliers.
  - **Absolute correlation ranges** (dict with any value > 10, e.g. `{'xy': 5000, 'z': 50}`) — raw coordinates are divided by these ranges so 1 unit ≈ 1 correlation range. This is the geostatistically proper mode for anisotropic data where horizontal and vertical scales differ by orders of magnitude.

Two helper functions were added:
- `_build_connectivity()` — builds a symmetric k-NN graph using `sklearn.neighbors.kneighbors_graph`.
- `_apply_connectivity_scale()` — handles the three scaling modes for the connectivity graph coordinates.

**2. `pingtung_lithology_nonstationary.ipynb` — Updated to use connectivity-constrained clustering**

Cell 8 (the `identify_homogeneous_regions_data` call) now passes:

```python
spatial_connectivity=True,
connectivity_k=8,
connectivity_scale={'xy': d_max_h, 'z': d_max_v},
```

This uses the horizontal and vertical max distances (`d_max_h` and `d_max_v`) from the Pmodel fitting as the absolute correlation ranges for the connectivity graph, ensuring the neighbourhood definition properly accounts for the distinct horizontal (~17 km) and vertical (~80 m) correlation scales.

The markdown description cell (cell 6) was also updated to document the connectivity-constrained approach.

            "text": "class GWPmodel:",
